content: Dover's Powder was a historical medicinal preparation used primarily for the treatment of colds and fevers. It is no longer utilized in contemporary medical practice. The powder was named after Dr. Thomas Dover, an English physician from the 18th century who originally formulated it. The composition of Dover's Powder included powdered ipecacuanha (a substance now used in the production of syrup of ipecac), powdered opium, and potassium sulfate. This preparation was widely employed in domestic medicine to induce sweating, which was believed to counteract the progression of a cold or to address the early stages of a fever. It was also referred to by its Latin name, Pulvis Ipecacuanhae et Opii. For optimal sudorific (sweat-inducing) effects, it was recommended that the powder be taken alongside generous amounts of a warm, harmless beverage. An example of its use is documented in a report by Dr. Sharp, a physician serving in the British naval forces in the West Indies, specifically in Trinidad, in 1818. Dr. Sharp described its application in the treatment of acute dysentery cases. He noted that, among thirty cases of acute dysentery, nineteen involved men who had recently arrived from Europe. Despite their recent arrival, the symptoms in these individuals were as mild as those in acclimatized soldiers. The disease responded well to standard treatments of the time, which included bloodletting when vascular conditions warranted it, as well as the administration of small, repeated doses of saline purgatives. In addition, small doses of calomel (mercurous chloride) and opium at bedtime, along with infusions of ipecacuanha or Dover's Powder, were commonly employed. These measures were supplemented with tonics, moderate consumption of port wine, and a light, farinaceous (starch-based) diet. This combination of treatments generally led to a rapid and complete recovery in most cases.
